Ramakrishna.description: A 19th-century Bengali mystic and saint, influential in the revival of Hinduism in India.

Swami Vivekananda.description: A prominent Indian monk and disciple of Ramakrishna, known for introducing Indian philosophies to the West.

Upanishads.description: Ancient Sanskrit texts that form the philosophical basis of Hinduism, focusing on meditation, morality, and spiritual knowledge.

Vedas.description: The oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, composed in Sanskrit and foundational to Indian spiritual thought.

Gurukul.description: A traditional Indian residential school where students live and learn with their teacher, often focused on spiritual and classical education.

Arya Samaj.description: A Hindu reform movement founded in the 19th century, advocating values based on the Vedas and social reform.

Sicily.description: An island region of Italy, referenced as part of Mircea's European memories.

Rome.description: The capital city of Italy, referenced for its ancient ruins.

Florence.description: A city in Italy, renowned for its art, architecture, and Renaissance history.

Switzerland.description: A European country, referenced for its solitude and scenic beauty.

Benares.description: A sacred city on the Ganges in India, known for its spiritual significance and also referred to as Varanasi or Kashi.

Je Alo Nibe Geche.description: A Bengali book title mentioned as authored by Mircea, meaning 'The Light That Has Been Extinguished.'

anklets.description: Traditional ornamental jewelry worn around the ankles, often associated with femininity and dance in Indian culture.

kohl.description: A black cosmetic applied around the eyes, commonly used in South Asia for both beauty and cultural reasons.

sadhana.description: A term for spiritual practice or disciplined effort undertaken to achieve spiritual realization.

mantras.description: Sacred utterances, sounds, or phrases repeated in meditation or spiritual practice in Hinduism and Buddhism.

lungi.description: A traditional garment, a loose cloth wrapped around the waist, commonly worn by men in South Asia.

karma.description: A concept in Indian religions referring to the law of moral cause and effect, where actions influence future outcomes.

rupees.description: The currency of India, referenced here as a sum of money requested by Khoka.

John.description: A newly acquainted companion of the narrator in Chicago who helps her navigate the city and reach Woodland Road.

Molly.description: A woman who assists Amrita upon her arrival, ensuring she is taken care of and arranging for her to meet others.

Sharly.description: A young student at the university who helps Amrita with directions and accompanies her to meet the professor; also spelled Sharly.

Ed.description: A person mentioned by Mircea as someone who supposedly informed him of Amrita's arrival.

Vishweshwara.description: A Sanskrit epithet meaning 'Lord of the Universe,' often used for the Hindu god Shiva.

pole star.description: A metaphor for steadfastness; in Indian tradition, the pole star (Dhruva Tara) symbolizes guidance and constancy.

Woodland Road.description: A street in Chicago that Amrita is trying to reach to meet her old acquaintance.

Theological College.description: A college or academic institution focused on the study of theology, referenced here as the place where Mircea works.

Holy Grail.description: A legendary object in Western mythology, symbolizing a highly sought-after goal; used metaphorically.

Sumeru.description: A sacred mountain in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist cosmology, considered the center of the universe.

Kali.description: A Hindu goddess associated with destruction, time, and transformation, often depicted as dark and powerful.

Dante.description: Dante Alighieri, the Italian poet, referenced for his love for Beatrice in 'The Divine Comedy.'

Beatrice.description: Dante's muse and symbol of idealized love in 'The Divine Comedy.'

Lake Michigan.description: One of the five Great Lakes of North America, located near Chicago.

Pandora’s box.description: A reference from Greek mythology, symbolizing the release of unforeseen troubles and hope.

Milky Way.description: The galaxy containing our solar system, used here as a poetic metaphor for a distant meeting place.

Nayantam na madhyam na punastavadim.description: A Sanskrit phrase meaning 'neither beginning nor middle nor end,' expressing the infinite nature of the divine.

pashyami Vishweshwara Vishwarupam.description: Sanskrit for 'I behold the Lord of the Universe in his cosmic form,' referencing a vision of divinity.

shastra chhede na, agni dohe na jare.description: A Bengali/Sanskrit phrase meaning 'weapons cannot pierce, fire cannot burn,' alluding to the immortal soul.

Na hanyate hanyamane sharire.description: Sanskrit for 'It does not die when the body is slain,' from the Bhagavad Gita, signifying the immortality of the soul.
